entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0412: Vulnerability in cargo-nextest
entry.summary: Arbitrary code execution when rerunning tests from a portable recording
entry.content:

Arbitrary code execution when rerunning tests from a portable recording

  • https://github.com/nextest-rs/nextest/commit/59ef7afc7887caea50aabed289756820e08f366a

CVSS Score

CVSS Vector
CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
Patched
  • >=0.9.150
Unaffected
  • <0.9.125

Description

Summary

Nextest versions between 0.9.125 and 0.9.149 (inclusive) allow the cargo nextest run --rerun (or -R) command with a malicious portable recording to run arbitrary code during the build. The result is arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running cargo nextest.

This vulnerability requires that the experimental run recording functionality is enabled. An attacker can plausibly trick a victim into enabling this feature.

Details

Nextest's portable recordings contain build scope arguments. These arguments are deserialized verbatim from portable recordings, and are not validated. As a result, it is possible to construct an archive with a custom --config argument that causes Cargo to execute arbitrary code.

Nextest 0.9.150 records the build scope as structured data, and passes each value to Cargo joined to its flag (for example, --package=<value>), so a recording can no longer add other Cargo options.

Impact

A malicious portable recording leads to arbitrary code execution as the user who runs cargo nextest run --rerun, during the build phase, before any test runs.

  • The injected configuration takes effect during cargo build, so the payload is run even on a warm build cache, and even when no tests are ultimately executed. Inspecting the recorded tests (with e.g. cargo nextest replay) before running them does not help, since the code has already run by the time the tests would start.
  • Arbitrary code execution happens as the invoking user, without a prompt or trust warning. The only signal is a rerun: inheriting build scope… line. On CI, this includes access to whatever secrets are accessible to the job, including repository tokens and deployment credentials.
  • A malicious payload can invoke the real compiler afterwards, so the build and tests complete normally. The recording is otherwise a valid, ordinary recording.
  • The full Cargo --config surface is exposed. This includes build.rustc-wrapper, build.rustc, target.*.linker, target.*.runner, env.*, and patch.* and source.*.replace-with (redirecting dependencies to an attacker-controlled repository or registry).
  • The delivery mechanism matches the feature's intended use, since portable recordings are designed to be shared across machines. For example, an attacker could pose as a user asking a maintainer for help triaging their flaky test report. Because --rerun also accepts process substitution, cargo nextest run --rerun <(curl …) would fetch the recording directly from a URL.

Exploitation requires convincing the victim to run cargo nextest run --rerun against an attacker-supplied portable recording. The rerun feature is experimental and must be enabled, via e.g. NEXTEST_EXPERIMENTAL_RECORD=1.

Remediations

  • Upgrade cargo-nextest to version 0.9.150 or above.
  • In your repositories, set the minimum required version to 0.9.150. In .config/nextest.toml: 
    nextest-version = "0.9.150"
    This way, anyone who interacts with your repository will be notified to upgrade their version of nextest.
  • If you are using an affected version, do not enable the experimental run recording feature.

Credit

Reported by inanna-malick.

RUSTSEC-2026-0393

Out-of-bounds read when training a dictionary from inconsistent sample sizes
Reported

Package
zstd (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
Categories
  • memory-exposure
Keywords
#integer-overflow #out-of-bounds #dictionary
References
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/commit/781ea454191dbf178d09c1daf6fc896d15fbaa2f
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/384
Patched
  • >=0.4.10
Unaffected
  • <0.1.1

Description

ZDICT_trainFromBuffer is never told the length of the samples buffer. Before 0.4.10, zstd::dict::from_continuous (initially train_dict) called it directly: up to 0.2.1 without checking the sample sizes against the buffer at all, and from 0.3.0 with a sum that wraps around when overflow checks are off, as in release builds. Sizes that do not describe the buffer made the trainer read past its end.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. From 0.4.10, training goes through zstd-safe, where the same flaw is covered by the zstd-safe advisory for it, fixed in zstd-safe 8.2.0.

entry.summary: Uninitialized memory exposed by `write::Decoder` on a corrupt legacy frame
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0392

Uninitialized memory exposed by write::Decoder on a corrupt legacy frame
Reported
October 16, 2026
Issued
October 26, 2026
Package
zstd (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • memory-exposure
Keywords
#uninitialized-memory #decompression #legacy
References
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/commit/006e1d1ad1eeaf6b5d4c28329e70217adabcec43
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/384
Patched
  • >=0.8.0
Unaffected
  • <0.4.22

Description

From 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, the writer behind zstd::stream::write::Decoder set its output buffer's length to its full capacity before each decompression call, then to the position the call reported, and only checked for an error afterwards. When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the bundled zstd library reports the output as fully written although nothing was written, so stale heap memory, up to the buffer size (32 KiB by default), was passed to the wrapped writer.

Legacy support is enabled by default, and a few bytes of corrupt legacy frame are enough. Whether this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the decompressed output.

From 0.8.0, the writer uses zstd-safe's buffers, and the same flaw there is covered by the zstd-safe advisory for it, fixed in zstd-safe 8.2.0.

RUSTSEC-2026-0391

Data from an abandoned stream leaks into the next stream on a reused context
Reported

Type

#information-leak #context-reuse
References
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/commit/74ace2dcdca62a2ce0f034895d6079458311e003
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/384
Patched
  • >=0.14.3
Unaffected
  • <0.13.2
Affected Functions
Version
zstd::stream::raw::Decoder::with_context
  • >=0.13.2, <0.14.3
zstd::stream::raw::Encoder::with_context
  • >=0.13.2, <0.14.3

Description

The with_context constructors of the stream encoders and decoders used the borrowed context as it was. When a stream was abandoned on a context, for example an encoder dropped before finish() after an error, whatever it left there was carried into the next stream: the input buffered by the previous encoder (up to 128 KiB, or all of it with zstdmt) became the start of the next frame, and a decoder returned undelivered output of the previous stream.

An application reusing one context for data that must stay separate, such as different users' requests, could disclose one user's plaintext to another. Whoever supplies the data can cause the abandonment with invalid input.

The flaw was corrected by resetting the context's session in with_context.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Patched
  • >=0.8.1

Description

Pingora versions prior to 0.8.1 used the h2 crate's default HTTP/2 server limits, a 16 MiB decoded header-list size and no limit on concurrent streams, unless the application set its own. A remote, unauthenticated client can send 1-byte HPACK references to a near-empty header, making the server allocate hundreds of thousands of header fields per stream across an unlimited number of streams on one connection, and use HTTP/2 flow control to keep those streams open. This can exhaust memory and degrade or terminate the Pingora process.

This affects any Pingora service that terminates HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) without explicitly setting max_header_list_size and max_concurrent_streams. The reporter showed that a single connection could get a Pingora process with a 2 GiB memory limit OOM-killed.

This flaw was corrected in commit d193c8d49b8b7c1c1ede93183759caa4f6906bbd. When no H2Options are supplied, Pingora now advertises and enforces a 64 KiB decoded header-list limit and at most 100 concurrent streams per connection. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.8.1. Applications that supply their own H2Options are not covered by these defaults and must set max_header_list_size and max_concurrent_streams explicitly, or start from pingora_core::protocols::http::v2::server::default_h2_options(). H2Options::default() does not include these limits.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Patched
  • >=0.9.0

Description

Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 accepted HTTP/2 requests whose Host header differed from the :authority pseudo-header. Request filters, cache keys, and logs that read the request URI (session.req_header().uri) saw the :authority value, but the upstream received the client-supplied Host value. Pingora also accepted :authority values containing userinfo (for example, user@example.com). This violates RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1, which requires an intermediary to use the :authority value for Host and replace any existing Host field.

A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a single HTTP/2 request that the application sees as one host and the upstream receives as another. Where request filters, access controls, or cache keys use the URI authority and the upstream routes by Host, this can lead to cache poisoning, where a response from another virtual host is stored under the victim host's cache key and served to other users, or host-based access control bypass, where a request approved for one host is served by a different virtual host on the upstream. Deployments that do not accept HTTP/2 from clients, or that do not use the request authority for security or caching decisions, are not affected.

This flaw was corrected in commits 915590a91811877795531f6ba0927a3138b5cb4b and ffab8302d08d4292d1924eb8fe84647fd5cb8e76. Pingora now returns 400 Bad Request for HTTP/2 requests whose Host differs from :authority, that contain more than one Host, or whose authority contains userinfo, and keeps the upstream Host or :authority consistent with the request authority. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.9.0.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as internal Pingora services at Cloudflare do not have HTTP/2 clients.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.summary: Build environment compiled into the library and readable at runtime
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0394

Build environment compiled into the library and readable at runtime
Reported
September 23, 2026

October 26, 2026
Package
rustpython-vm (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Keywords
#information-disclosure #build-script #credentials
References
  • https://github.com/RustPython/RustPython/pull/8813
  • https://github.com/RustPython/RustPython/issues/8802
  • https://github.com/RustPython/RustPython/issues/9236
  • https://crates.io/crates/rustpython-vm/0.6.0
  • https://registry.bitbison.io/cargo/rustpython-vm
Patched
  • >=0.6.0
Unaffected
  • <0.3.0

Description

The build script of rustpython-vm 0.3.0 through 0.5.0 writes every environment variable of the build into $OUT_DIR/env_vars.rs. The crate compiles that file into _sysconfigdata's build_time_vars. That module is always compiled.

A binary built in CI with secrets in the environment carries those secrets in clear text. Registry tokens, cloud credentials and API keys are the usual ones. Anyone with the binary can read them with strings or from Python.

Version 0.6.0 removes the dump and the include. Users of earlier versions should upgrade, rebuild, and ship new binaries. Every secret that was in the environment of a past build whose output left the build machine should be treated as exposed.

Jacob Finkelman first reported the issue in #8802. Bitbison's automated supply chain scanning then detected credential data from the build environment flowing into artifacts that third-party software ships in the wild. The leak was confirmed in the published release binaries of at least four dependants but others have been impacted.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

RUSTSEC-2026-0395

Use-after-free with CParameter::StableInBuffer
Reported

Type

#use-after-free #experimental
References
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/commit/53a8a290d8cfb52ff5b29fb6e04a40b5a174cc65
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/384
Patched
  • >=8.2.0
Unaffected
  • <4.1.0
Affected Functions
Version
zstd_safe::CCtx::set_parameter
  • >=4.1.0, <8.2.0

Description

With CParameter::StableInBuffer(true) (experimental feature), the C library keeps a pointer to the input of one streaming call and reads from it in later calls, including flush_stream and end_stream, which take no input. An InBuffer only borrows its slice for one call, so safe code could free it in between, and freed memory was compressed into the frame. The C library behaves this way since zstd 1.5.4, whether bundled or linked from the system.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to enable the parameter.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Seekable::decompress sets a Vec length beyond its capacity for offsets past the end
Reported

Type
Vulnerability

Patched

Unaffected

Affected Functions
Version
zstd_safe::seekable::AdvancedSeekable::decompress
  • >=7.2.2, <8.2.0
zstd_safe::seekable::Seekable::decompress
  • >=7.2.2, <8.2.0

Description

ZSTD_seekable_decompress shortens the requested length to the end of the data without checking that the offset is before it. For an offset past the end, it returns a wrapped-around length without writing anything, and Seekable::decompress passed that length to Vec::set_len.

With the seekable feature, whoever supplies the archive, or chooses the offset, can leave the caller's Vec<u8> with a length far beyond its capacity. Reading it then discloses neighbouring heap memory, and appending to it corrupts memory. Offsets near u64::MAX can also hang the call.

The flaw was corrected by clamping requests to the end of the data, and by checking every count reported by the C library against the buffer capacity.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.summary: Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0406

Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame
Reported
October 16, 2026
Issued
October 26, 2026
Package
zstd-safe (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
Categories
  • memory-corruption
Keywords
#use-after-free #zstdmt #dictionary
References
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/commit/e224018a2389915d68ed17f30109bebad36e9734
  • https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/pull/384
Patched
  • >=8.2.0
Affected Functions
Version
zstd_safe::CCtx::disable_dictionary
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::init
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::load_dictionary
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::ref_cdict
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::ref_prefix
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::reset
  • <8.2.0
zstd_safe::CCtx::set_parameter
  • <8.2.0

Description

When a multithreaded frame (zstdmt feature, CParameter::NbWorkers) is left unfinished, its jobs may still be running on the worker threads: the C library only waits for them when the next frame starts, or when the context is freed. A session reset makes the context accept changes again in the meantime, so:

  • unloading the dictionary (load_dictionary, ref_cdict, ref_prefix, disable_dictionary, init*, or reset with parameters) freed the dictionary a worker was still compressing against;
  • changing NbWorkers made the next frame resize the job table before waiting for the old jobs.

The flaw was corrected by refusing these calls while a multithreaded frame is unfinished. The new CCtx::wait_for_workers() waits for the workers first.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

RUSTSEC-2025-0173

PamHandle::get_user can cause an authentication bypass
Reported

October 26, 2026
Package
pam-bindings (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • privilege-escalation
Keywords
#pam #authentication #ffi #undefined-behavior
References
  • https://github.com/lvkv/pam-rs/issues/16
Patched
  • >=0.1.2

Description

In affected versions, PamHandle::get_user can return Err(PAM_SUCCESS) after it gets the username successfully. PAM modules that return this "error" code from sm_authenticate or sm_acct_mgmt early-return a success code to PAM without doing any further verification. This means a user could log in when they shouldn't be able to (e.g., if the module is sufficient).

The pam_try! macro of this crate early-returns the code in this exact way:

fn sm_authenticate(pamh: &mut PamHandle, args: Vec<&CStr>, flags: PamFlag) -> PamResultCode {
    let user = pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None)); // Can return PAM_SUCCESS here.
    // If it does, the module does not get to this line.
}

The root cause is an incorrect FFI declaration for pam_get_user(3). This C function writes a pointer to the username through its user argument (of type const char **user). This crate's binding declared this argument as a shared reference (&*mut c_char). Writing through a shared reference is undefined behavior.

Thus, the compiler can assume that the local pointer, whose address is passed as user, is still null after the call. After the call, the affected code returns Ok only if the return code is PAM_SUCCESS and this pointer is not null. Otherwise, it returns the return code as an error. If the compiler assumes that the pointer is null, get_user returns an error even when the return code is PAM_SUCCESS. Release builds have been observed to do this. Debug builds usually work correctly, so tests in debug mode can miss the problem.

Version 0.1.2 changes the declaration to &mut *const c_char. The fix is in commit 401c961.

If a module cannot upgrade, do not return the error code from get_user. Return a failure code instead, for example pam_try!(pamh.get_user(None), PamResultCode::PAM_AUTH_ERR). This makes the module deny access instead of allowing it, but the undefined behavior remains.

Description

OrderedSkipList, SkipSet and SkipMap can free a node that is still linked when a Comparator or Ord implementation gives different answers for the same pair of values during one mutating call. A later call reads the freed memory (CWE-416). A safe impl Ord with the default comparator is enough to reach it.

The mutating traversals record a precursor at each level: the last node whose link points at a node comparing not-Less than the target. The splice code assumes every recorded precursor's link points at or past the final position. If a later comparison reports one of those nodes as Less, the walk steps past it and the assumption breaks. Removals such as take_first, take and remove then rewire the wrong link and free the target while its real predecessor still points at it. insert builds crossed links and wrong skip distances from the same precursors.

A comparator that is a pure function of its two arguments cannot trigger this, even if it is not transitive. The trigger is a stateful or non-deterministic implementation, for example one that reads a counter, a cache, a clock or a random source.

The flaw was corrected in 1.3.0. The mutating traversals track the link target of the lowest recorded precursor and panic with "comparator does not implement a total order" when a Less answer contradicts an earlier one. Every splice site also checks its precursors before the first write. Each detected contradiction panics before any link, value or length changes, so the collection stays valid and safe to drop.

Description

Pingora versions prior to 0.9.0 passed the downstream request through upstream_request_filter and wrote it to HTTP/1 upstreams without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominated, although RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1 requires intermediaries to remove them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers. A client could therefore nominate a header that the application adds in upstream_request_filter (for example, Connection: keep-alive, X-Forwarded-For). A downstream HTTP/1 intermediary that honors Connection would then strip the Pingora-added header before it reached the origin.

This specifically affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin processes Connection nominations (for example, Go's net/http/httputil.ReverseProxy) and the origin trusts headers added by that intermediary (for example, X-Forwarded-For for IP-based authorization). A remote, unauthenticated attacker can have those headers removed, potentially bypassing authorization. This is the same class of issue as CVE-2022-31813 in Apache HTTP Server.

This flaw was corrected in commits 28c18e6b6b04dd0bd937234e5950049e6d74cded and ca23f1668eca8e78be7ba62ef0edbd458b40eeee. By default, Pingora now removes hop-by-hop and Connection-nominated headers from upstream requests, and rejects requests whose Connection header nominates Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, or a pseudo-header. This is controlled by PeerOptions::http_upstream_request_policy; HttpUpstreamRequestPolicy::preserve() restores the old passthrough behavior and should not be used if the origin relies on headers added by Pingora. Users should upgrade to Pingora >= 0.9.0.

Note: Cloudflare CDN customers were unaffected, as no such chained deployment as described above exists with internal Pingora services, and Connection headers are sanitized before arriving at Pingora gateways.

History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0411

Out-of-bounds read in Log2Cache::nlog2n(), nlog2n_difference() and plog2p()
Reported
October 22, 2026
Issued
October 26, 2026
Package
dahl-salso (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
Categories
  • memory-corruption
  • memory-exposure
Keywords
#out-of-bounds #unsound
References
  • https://github.com/dbdahl/rust-dahl-salso/issues/2
Patched
  • >=0.7.0

Description

Log2Cache::new(n) fills its three tables with entries for 0..=n, but the three accessor methods index those tables with get_unchecked on a value the caller supplies. Nothing bounds the argument and nothing documents a bound, so any value above the n the cache was built with reads past the end of the vector. CountType is u32, so the read can land up to u32::MAX elements away, and plog2p() returns the value it read, disclosing whatever lies there.

For example, Log2Cache::new(4) builds tables holding 5 entries (indices 0,1,2,3,4). Then cache.nlog2n(60000) reads index 60000, far outside the allocation. Under AddressSanitizer this faults with SEGV; Miri reports it as undefined behavior at src/log2cache.rs:42.

nlog2n_difference() is off by one further: in the affected versions new(n) pushes n entries into that table rather than n + 1, so even nlog2n_difference(n) is out of bounds.

This can be triggered through safe public APIs — Log2Cache::new() and any of nlog2n(), nlog2n_difference() and plog2p() — with no unsafe required from the caller.

entry.summary: Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0387

Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time
Reported

October 23, 2026

crypto-bigint (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • crypto-failure
References
  • https://github.com/RustCrypto/crypto-bigint/pull/1365
Patched
  • >=0.7.6

Description

Summary

Several operations intended to be constant-time could execute secret-dependent branches, depending on the compiler and target CPU. These include subtraction, zero counting, division, and Montgomery multiplication.

Additionally, UintRef equality could terminate at the first unequal limb, and BoxedMontyForm::invert branched on whether an inverse exists.

Impact

Applications using affected operations on secret integers may leak information through timing or microarchitectural side channels. This includes information about intermediate arithmetic values, matching limbs, and invertibility.

Such leakage could potentially enable recovery of cryptographic secrets. Practical exploitability depends on the downstream algorithm, compiler, target CPU, and an attacker's ability to observe the side channel.

Resolution

Upgrade to v0.7.6, which removes the identified branches, updates ctutils to include its constant-time fixes, and adds BINSEC-based regression checks using cargo checkct for arithmetic on multiple targets.

entry.summary: Non-constant-time mask generation and `u128` comparisons

Non-constant-time mask generation and u128 comparisons
Reported
October 23, 2026

October 23, 2026

ctutils (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability

  • crypto-failure
References
  • https://github.com/RustCrypto/utils/pull/1569
Related

Patched
  • >=0.4.4

Description

Summary

The ctutils::Choice type has mask generation functions for each unsigned integer size (u8, u16, u32, u64, u128). These are const fn and therefore can't reuse the asm!-backed mask generation in the cmov crate that's otherwise used to ensure constant-time.

In releases prior to v0.4.4, the generated code from these functions could include a branch on commonly used platforms. This has been corrected in this release and now verified on several platforms using BINSEC.

Additionally, u128 comparison operations provided via ctutils::Choice and intended to work in constant-time were generating branches on 32-bit targets. This has been resolved via a special case implementation of these functions for such targets.

Impact

Branch instructions on secret values can potentially leak such values via covert channels. This can enable attackers to potentially recover such secrets.

Resolution

This has been resolved by calling Choice::to_u8() when generating the mask, which in turn uses black_box as an optimization barrier. Verification that this resulted in the desired change in the generated assembly across a variety of target CPU architectures was performed by BINSEC, which now runs automatically in CI using cargo checkct.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0386: Unsoundness in tokio
entry.summary: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0386

AsyncFd::new and related constructors violate I/O safety
Reported
October 13, 2026
Issued
October 23, 2026
Package
tokio (crates.io)
Type
INFO Unsound
Categories
  • memory-corruption
Keywords
#io-safety #use-after-free
References
  • https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8587
  • https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/8538
  • https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/8539
Patched
  • >=1.51.6, <1.52.0
  • >=1.53.3
Unaffected
  • <0.3.2
Affected Functions
Version
tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::new
  • >=0.3.2
tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::try_new
  • >=1.37.0
tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::try_with_interest
  • >=1.37.0
tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd::with_interest
  • >=0.3.2

Description

tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd provides safe constructors (new, with_interest, try_new, and try_with_interest) that accept any T: AsRawFd rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because RawFd implements AsRawFd, safe code can construct an AsyncFd from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the AsyncFd is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

  1. AsyncFd<T> implements AsFd for all T: AsRawFd by calling BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd()), allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary BorrowedFd<'_> without owning the file descriptor.
  2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the epoll/kqueue user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an AsyncFd is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first AsyncFd deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in epoll, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, AsyncFd::new, AsyncFd::with_interest, AsyncFd::try_new, and AsyncFd::try_with_interest are deprecated in favor of the unsafe constructors AsyncFd::register and AsyncFd::register_with_interest. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the AsyncFd.

RUSTSEC-2026-0384

Race condition in tokio::time::Interval on Tokio v1.54.0

References

Patched

Unaffected
  • <1.54.0

Description

Summary

On the multi-threaded runtime, there is a race condition between Interval::poll_tick and the runtime's time driver.

This affects Interval only. Sleep and Timeout are not affected.

Details

In Tokio v1.54.0, a race condition between tokio::time::Interval::poll_tick (including .tick().await) and the runtime time driver can drop an internal timer entry without synchronizing with the driver thread that is firing it. This causes a data race and use-after-free on the timer's waker and task state in safe Rust, leading to assertion panics, task reference-count corruption, or heap memory corruption.

This bug was introduced by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8458, and it was fixed by https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/pull/8692.

Impact

This may lead to crashes and use-after-frees in applications using Interval on a multi-threaded runtime.

Since this issue is known to lead to crashes in production systems, the v1.54.0 release of Tokio has been yanked.

Credits

Thank you to creepycode and carabistouille for reporting this privately using the procedure outlined in our security policy. They both reported the issue independently of each other.
